notes.meaning: Some time later, Jesus showed Himself to His disciples again. This time it was by the Sea of Tiberias, which is another name for the Sea of Galilee. John tells this story with care because it gives more proof that Jesus really rose from the dead. After rising, Jesus appeared to His friends now and then, often when they did not expect Him.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some critics have argued that this chapter was added later by a different writer, because the end of chapter 20 sounds like the close of the book.

notes.meaning: Seven disciples were together. Nathanael may be the same man the other Gospels call Bartholomew. The two who are not named may have been Andrew and Philip. Thomas, who once doubted, is now staying close to the group. Having several people there meant they could all be witnesses to what happened.

Peter decided to go fishing, and the others went with him. This was not a wrong step. They were waiting for Jesus and had not yet been sent out to preach, and they needed to earn a living. They caught nothing all night. God allowed this so the miracle that came next would stand out even more.

At dawn Jesus stood on the shore, but the disciples did not know it was Him. The light may still have been dim, He was some way off, or their eyes may have been kept from seeing Him clearly. Christ is often nearer to us than we think.

Jesus called out to them with a friendly word, much like saying "lads" or "my boys." He asked whether they had caught any fish. He already knew the answer, but He wanted them to admit they had nothing. In this way He showed He cares about His people's everyday needs, even food.

The disciples did what the stranger said, and the net filled with so many fish they could not pull it in. The catch showed Jesus' power and also met their real needs. It pictured their future work too, as "fishers of men," meaning people who bring others to Jesus. It recalls a similar catch at the start of His ministry (Luke 5).

John, "the disciple whom Jesus loved," was the first to see that it was the Lord. Peter was the first to rush to Him. He had stripped down to his work clothes, so he put on his outer coat out of respect and jumped into the water. John was quick to see and Peter was quick to act, and both showed real love for Jesus.

The other disciples stayed in the boat and dragged the heavy net about a hundred yards to shore. They came more slowly than Peter, but they still came to Christ. Some believers serve Jesus with bold, eager acts. Others serve by faithfully doing the needed work, and He accepts both.

On shore they found a charcoal fire with fish cooking on it, and some bread. We are not told where it came from. Some think Jesus made it by a miracle, while others see no need to think so. Either way, it shows the Lord's kind care for His tired, hungry friends. The charcoal fire may also remind readers of the fire where Peter had denied Jesus.

Jesus asked them to bring some of the fish they had just caught. He did not need their fish, because breakfast was already cooking. He let them share in what came from their own work, even though the catch was really His gift. In the same way, we call our daily food "our bread," while knowing it comes from God.

Peter pulled the net to shore by himself, though earlier they could not haul it in. It held 153 large fish. Fishermen would count such an unusual catch, so the number is simply what they counted, with no hidden code. Even with so many fish the net did not tear, which was part of the miracle. In the same way, the gospel "net" has gathered huge numbers of people and is still as strong as ever.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine saw a hidden meaning in the number. He took 10 for the Law and 7 for the Holy Spirit, which makes 17, and adding every number from 1 to 17 gives 153.

notes.meaning: Jesus warmly invited them to breakfast. None of them dared to ask, "Who are You?" because they already knew it was the Lord. After such clear signs, asking would have seemed like doubting Him. They felt both joy and deep respect in His presence.

Jesus acted as host. He took the bread and fish and handed it to each of them. Being with them, eating with them and serving them helped prove that He had truly risen with a real body. He was the same Friend who had died.

John notes that this was the third time Jesus had appeared to a group of His disciples together after rising from the dead. Jesus had also appeared to some people on their own. He came again and again to make His friends sure that He was alive.

After breakfast, Jesus spoke to Peter alone. He called him "Simon," his old name, perhaps as a gentle reminder that he had not stood firm like a rock. "More than these" most likely means "more than the other disciples do." Peter had once boasted that he would never fall away, even if all the others did, though some think it means "more than your boats and nets." Peter now answers humbly. He makes no comparison and simply trusts that Jesus knows his heart. Jesus then gives him a job: care for His "lambs," the young and new believers.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching sees Jesus here giving Peter alone the leadership of His whole flock, and holds that this role passes down to the bishops of Rome (the popes). Catholics agree the scene makes up for Peter's denials. But they argue that since all the disciples ran away, singling out Peter must point to a unique role.

notes.meaning: Jesus asked a second time, now leaving out "more than these." Peter gave the same humble answer. This time Jesus said "Shepherd My sheep," which means more than feeding. It covers all of a shepherd's work: guiding, protecting and leading the whole church.

When Jesus asked a third time, Peter was hurt. The question reminded him of the three times he had denied Jesus, and he may have feared he would fail again. He answered, "Lord, You know all things," trusting Jesus to see his heart. Three questions matched three denials, so Peter could be sure he was forgiven and given back his work as an apostle, one of the twelve Jesus sent out. The same task of caring for Christ's people belongs to all of His ministers, not to Peter alone.

Jesus told Peter what lay ahead. When Peter was young, he dressed himself and went where he liked. When he was old, others would tie him up and lead him where he did not want to go, to a violent death. "Stretch out your hands" is often seen as a hint of crucifixion, and early tradition says Peter was crucified in Rome. "Where you do not want to go" does not mean Peter would be unwilling to die for Jesus. It speaks of the natural fear of death that even faithful believers feel.

John explains that Jesus was pointing to the kind of death by which Peter would bring honor to God. Peter would become a martyr, someone who dies for his faith. Then Jesus said, "Follow Me." These were the same words He used when He first called Peter. Now they also meant: follow Me, even to a death like Mine.

Peter turned and saw John following them. John describes himself as the one who leaned against Jesus at the Last Supper. That was when John asked, at Peter's request, who would betray Jesus. This may explain why Peter now asks about John. The scene also warns us that looking around at others can pull us away from our own calling.

Peter asked, "Lord, what about him?" He probably wanted to know how John would die. He may have asked out of care for his friend, or out of simple curiosity after hearing his own hard future. Whatever the reason, Jesus chose not to satisfy that curiosity.

Jesus answered that even if He wanted John to live until He returned, that was not Peter's concern. Peter's job was to follow Jesus himself. This is a gentle but firm correction: mind your own calling, not someone else's. It also shows that Jesus holds the right to decide each person's life and death. Some have thought it hints that John would live a long time, outlasting the other apostles.

Among the early Christians, called "the brothers," a rumor spread that John would never die. John corrects it by repeating exactly what Jesus said, and no more. The lesson is to stay close to Jesus' actual words and not trust sayings that get passed around. Ancient writers say John later died peacefully at Ephesus.

The disciple whom Jesus loved, John, is the one who saw these things and wrote them down. He wrote as an eyewitness, not from hearsay. "We know his testimony is true" may be John speaking modestly about himself. Or it may be church leaders who knew him adding their own word that he told the truth.

Jesus did far more than this book records. Saying the world could not hold all the books is a figure of speech that says more than the literal words to make a point: there would be an enormous number of them. What God gave us is enough to lead us to believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and to find life in Him. We can be thankful for what is written and look forward to knowing more in heaven.
